ch12.note: A jia (枷), a heavy square wooden collar locked about a prisoner's neck like a portable pillory, worn day and night as punishment and public shaming in imperial China.

In Chinese folk-Buddhist belief the underworld descends through eighteen courts of torment, the eighteenth being the deepest and most terrible; to be cast into it is to sink to the lowest pit of suffering and disgrace.

ch12.anchor: the dagger showing at the map's end
ch12.note: The idiom tu qiong bi xian (图穷匕见), 'the map unrolled to its end, the dagger appears': at the failed assassination of the King of Qin in 227 BC, the envoy Jing Ke hid a blade inside a rolled map and drew it only as the map ran out—hence a hidden design laid bare at the last moment.

ch12.anchor: Virtue is not left an orphan; it must have neighbors
ch12.note: A saying of Confucius from the Analects (4.25): 'The virtuous is never left alone; he is sure to have neighbors'—goodness draws others to itself and never stands friendless.
Here 'the European war' means the First World War (1914–18), not the Second: the remembered meeting it dates belongs to the mid-1910s.

'Yu' (渝) is the traditional one-character name for Chongqing, the wartime capital. Chinese cities carry such single-character tags—Ping for Beiping, Jin for Tianjin, Hu for Shanghai, Yu for Chongqing—and the book uses them freely.

Lin Sen (林森, 1868–1943), Chairman of the National Government from 1931 to 1943—the ceremonial head of state of the Republic, a dignified figurehead while real power lay with Chiang Kai-shek, which is why the colorless 'Chairman Lin,' not Chiang, presides at a state rite.

ch12.anchor: the stair heard creaking, and no one coming down
ch12.note: From the proverb 'you hear the stairs creak, but nobody comes down' (只闻楼梯响，不见人下来): much noise and rumor of a thing about to happen, and then nothing at all.
